title: Output to Outcome, Ch 1: AI Won't Fix Your Company If the Bottleneck Isn't Code
description: Episode 2 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 1, "Product Operating Model," opens Part I, "Outcome Management," and is the first of the book's three foundational models, before the Outcome Loop (Ch 2) and the Outcome Tree (Ch 3). Kersten argues that AI's tenfold boost to coding won't help companies whose bottleneck sits elsewhere. In his State of the Industry data, only 8% of the time from idea to running software went to building it. We cover the Theory of Constraints and the jammed on-ramp, the history from McCallum's org chart to Gantt charts, Snowden's Cynefin framework and when to run a project versus a product, irreducible uncertainty and where AI can augment but not replace decisions, Reinertsen's life cycle profitability, the operating-model dysfunctions in Kersten's reports, and Commonwealth Bank of Australia's path from project to product to AI-native engineering. title: Output to Outcome, Ch 2: The Outcome Loop: Constraints, AI Surplus, and the Next Bottleneck
description: Episode 3 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 2, "The Outcome Loop," sits in the middle of Part I, "Outcome Management." It builds on Chapter 1's Product Operating Model, sets up Chapter 3's Outcome Tree, and is the core model that the book's seven shifts in Part II build on. Kersten defines the loop as the feedback system that connects inputs (strategy and budget) to outputs (activities and artifacts) to outcomes (employee, customer and business) and back again. We cover production elasticity and Amazon, the lineage from outcome-based healthcare and Jobs to Be Done to OKRs, Kersten's own path from PhD research to Tasktop, key results versus KPIs, the TeenWellness worked example, why the loop is a hypothesis test, broken telemetry and the "counting procedures" trap, applying the Theory of Constraints, and how the VS Code team's bottleneck moved from delivery to onboarding to code review as AI took over more of the output. Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. title: Output to Outcome, Ch 3: The Outcome Tree: Scaling AI-Era Orgs Like Redwoods, Not Waterfalls
description: Episode 4 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 3, "The Outcome Tree," is the last of Part I's three foundational models, after the Product Operating Model and the Outcome Loop. We also cover the short Conclusion to Part I, which previews the book's seven shifts. Kersten's question is how to scale one Outcome Loop to hundreds or thousands of value streams. We cover the "AI in Waterfall" dysfunction, the coordination math (n times n minus one connections), matrix overlays, Kotter's "second operating system," Holacracy and Haier's RenDanHeYi, and Geoffrey West's sublinear and superlinear scaling. We also cover the nature behind the model: redwoods, fractals, insulin and abscisic acid. Then the tree itself, with value streams as leaves, MECE partitioning, objective and budget cascades, and branching factors. Finally, Kersten's own path from Xerox PARC and AspectJ to building the Outcome Tree at Tasktop with help from Adrian Cockcroft and the Reverse Conway Maneuver, and his speculative idea of "organization as code." title: Output to Outcome, Ch 0: When AI Removes the Bottleneck: From Outputs to Outcomes
description: Episode 1 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 0, "Foundations," comes after the Preface, Prompt and Introduction and before Part I's three models: the Product Operating Model, the Outcome Loop and the Outcome Tree. Kersten argues that AI is making knowledge output nearly free, which moves the bottleneck from producing work to the organization itself. We cover the productivity paradox, the Theory of Constraints (and the car-plant paint shop), the earlier shift to software as a service, Carlota Perez's model of technological revolutions and her "golden age," the "three million Shakespeare plays" problem, and Kersten's account of Cognition's weekly outcome loop, where it throws away much of its code. We also cover the risk he warns about: AI's gains piling up in a few giants. Built from an IntuiBloom knowledge graph. title: Output to Outcome, Ch 4: From Silos to Value Streams: How AI Rewires the Org Chart
description: Episode 5 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 4 opens Part II, "The Seven Shifts," with the first shift: Functions to Flow. After Part I's three models (the Product Operating Model, the Outcome Loop and the Outcome Tree), Kersten argues that organizing around functional silos stops working when AI extends everyone's reach across domains. We cover handoffs and wait states, Priceline's drop from fifteen handoffs to five, and the Dedicated Leadership Model, Amazon's Single-Threaded Owners and Leaders, and single-, dual- and triple-leader structures. We also cover Kersten's claim that AI makes single leaders viable in more cases. Then value stream scope and "independence of action," SLAs for supporting functions, Value Stream Management and its lean manufacturing roots, capacity-based funding, and Weighted Shortest Job First. Finally, the TUI Group case: flow time cut from two hundred days to fifteen, a four-level AI literacy ladder, more than three thousand internal agents, and managers moving from owning people to owning outcomes. title: Output to Outcome, Ch 5: AI Made Output Cheap. Now Only Outcomes Matter
description: Episode 6 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 5, "Slop to Substance," is the second of Part II's seven shifts, after Chapter 4's move from functions to flow. Kersten argues that when AI makes output nearly unlimited, output metrics turn into vanity metrics, and only outcomes tell you whether work matters. We cover local optimization, Outcome Loop telemetry, and Strategic Portfolio Management. Then Plan Distribution (planned, unplanned, canceled and aged work, with only 25% of studied work aligned to strategy) and Goodhart's Law. Then the four Flow Items (features, defects, risks and debts), Flow Distribution, feature factories and the tech debt death spiral. Then the Flow Metrics Model: flow time, velocity, load and efficiency, and why not to use it on individuals. We also cover capacity planning from historical velocity, outcome metrics and attribution, Theory of Constraints, improvement objectives paired with employee happiness, agents that inspect Outcome Loops, and Vanguard's "Ideation Cliff." title: Output to Outcome, Ch 6: One Cadence to Rule Them All: AI's Real Operating System
description: Episode 7 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 6, "Chaos to Cadence," is the third of Part II's seven shifts, after Functions to Flow and Slop to Substance. Kersten asks why billion-dollar Agile and AI transformations can leave companies feeling slower. His answers: missing outcome measurement, and Agile layered onto legacy planning as a "second operating system." We cover the tree whose leaves photosynthesize faster than its trunk can carry, coordination cost, and the Unified Cadence Model of shared annual, quarterly, monthly and weekly cycles. We also cover planning against fixed historical capacity, roadmap autonomy with visible dependencies, and the recursive planning cascade down the Outcome Tree. Then the inputs, outputs and outcomes value stream report (including AI token spend), calendar-aligned planning, and the merger of Planview's and Tasktop's cadences, where moving to one cadence cut meeting and reporting overhead in half. title: Output to Outcome, Ch 7: From Messy Matrix to Modularity: Wiring Your Org for the Age of AI
description: Episode 8 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 7, "Matrix to Modularity," is the fourth of Part II's seven shifts, after Functions to Flow, Slop to Substance and Chaos to Cadence. Kersten argues that matrix and "dotted line" reporting creates a messy matrix of slow decisions, and that the fix is modular value streams built for independence of action. We cover high cohesion and low coupling (with LEGO, Linux and Google's overlapping messaging apps), Conway's Law and sociotechnical congruence, and the embed-versus-depend tradeoff. We also cover why improvement work belongs on the common parent's roadmap, one complexity domain per team, and Carliss Baldwin's option value. Then agents owning whole value streams, parallel hypothesis testing, John Lewis Partnership cutting delivery from ten days to 1.3, and Priceline's "Operating Model testing" taking complex flows from fifteen handoffs to five. title: Output to Outcome, Ch 8: Who Owns the Outcome? The Hidden Cost of Shared Accountability
description: Episode 9 of our book-club series on Mik Kersten's "Output to Outcome: An Operating Model for the Age of AI" (IT Revolution, 2026). Chapter 8, "Objectives to Ownership," is the fifth of Part II's seven shifts, after Functions to Flow, Slop to Substance, Chaos to Cadence and Matrix to Modularity. Kersten argues that ownership is the main control mechanism of the Outcome Tree, and that functional, matrix and shared ownership all diffuse accountability. We cover the Outcome Ownership Model, matching leaders' incentives one to one with their value stream's objectives, and turning priority order into incentive weights. We also cover why shared objectives are a trap (with Google's named owners and Apple's directly responsible individuals), aligning title levels to the tree, and title imbalance in dual-leader pairs. Then technical program managers and AI for dependency scenarios, the five-by-five limit on objectives and key results, and 70% stretch goals. Finally, Kersten's post-ChatGPT reorganization at Planview into a three-in-the-box AI value stream, and the later move, like GitHub Copilot's, to spread AI engineers into product teams.
